Poisson autoregression (PAR) models are designed to handle count data exhibiting serial dependence. This paper introduces a time-varying extension of the PAR framework, termed TVPAR, which allows regression coefficients to evolve over time. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the process under specific conditions and develop a Bayesian approach for parameter estimation. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through both simulated data and an analysis of daily traffic accident counts in New York City.

This study introduces a novel approach to measuring aerosol optical depth (AOD) by leveraging stellar photometry. The method relies on detecting the attenuation of starlight caused by atmospheric aerosols. We present the theoretical framework, detailing the mathematical relationships between observed stellar magnitudes and AOD. Furthermore, we describe the practical implementation of this technique using the ASPEEC instrument, which operates at the Palomar 2-meter telescope. The paper also outlines the data processing workflow required to convert photometric observations into precise AOD values. Finally, we demonstrate the method's efficacy through a case study of measurements taken during the 2019 Asian Dust Event, comparing our results against those from established ground-based networks and satellite data.

This study introduces a novel, efficient, and robust configurational molecular sampling method based on the Langevin integrator. The approach combines a multiple time step strategy with a specific, efficient scheme for handling the friction term. We demonstrate that this method achieves optimal convergence rates for both position and momentum variables, with the latter depending on the friction coefficient. Furthermore, the method maintains a convergence rate of $O(\Delta t)$ for the Boltzmann distribution, regardless of the friction coefficient's value. We validate the method's efficiency and robustness through extensive tests on various molecular systems, including water, alanine dipeptide, and the KDP crystal.

Evaluating the quality of automatic image descriptions (AIDs) is crucial for advancing the field, yet it remains challenging because no single evaluation metric has been universally accepted. While various methods exist, most rely on human reference data to establish ground truth. This study investigates the impact of using human references for AID evaluation, specifically examining how the selection of reference data influences the resulting quality scores. We conducted an analysis using the Flickr30k dataset, comparing descriptions generated by two distinct models: one trained exclusively on Flickr30k and another trained on the larger MS-COCO dataset. Our findings reveal that the choice of reference data significantly affects evaluation outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that descriptions produced by the Flickr30k-trained model are rated higher when evaluated against Flickr30k references compared to when evaluated against MS-COCO references, even though the MS-COCO-trained model generates superior descriptions overall. These results indicate that the choice of reference data introduces a bias, favoring models trained on the same source. Consequently, we recommend that future evaluations of AIDs utilize reference data from a broader, more diverse dataset to ensure fairer and more robust assessments.

We introduce a novel approach to calculating the complexity of conformal field theories (CFTs) by utilizing the Euler-Arnold equations. These equations govern the time evolution of the complexity for a generic CFT, which is defined as the minimal geodesic distance in the space of quantum circuits connecting two states. The solution to these equations is expressed through a closed-form formula involving the logarithmic derivative of the associated prepotential. This prepotential is identified with the two-dimensional topological sigma model defined on the target manifold of the CFT. We demonstrate the validity of this solution by applying it to free scalar fields, where the result aligns with the findings from the AdS/CFT correspondence.

This study examines the consequences of a specific extension to the Standard Model, which incorporates a new SU(2) gauge symmetry and introduces a single additional quark doublet. The analysis demonstrates that this framework predicts the existence of new baryons and mesons, alongside the anticipated discovery of new heavy gauge bosons. Furthermore, the paper outlines the anticipated decay modes for these newly predicted particles.

This study examines the optimal wideband waveforming strategies for integrated data and energy transfer (IDET) within SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. These serve as counterparts to the main analysis, which focused on a general wideband waveforming framework for IDET. The research demonstrates that the proposed SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations achieve performance levels that surpass those of traditional SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM methods. These enhanced results are attained without requiring additional hardware or energy expenditures.

This paper introduces a Python package designed to streamline the integration of theoretical predictions into Parton Distribution Function (PDF) fitting frameworks. The package offers a unified interface for various theoretical prediction tools, enabling the generation of a single, cohesive dataset for fitting procedures. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by fitting the CT18 parton distribution functions.

This study introduces a linearized model designed to predict the response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic forcing. The approach combines a linearized version of the G-equation with a linearized reaction rate formulation, both derived from an active flame framework. The model is validated against direct numerical simulation (DNS) results for a methane-air jet flame subjected to acoustic forcing at the nozzle inlet. The findings demonstrate that the linearized model accurately predicts the flame's response to acoustic forcing, with the linearized reaction rate formulation playing a crucial role in capturing the observed dynamics. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the flame's response is primarily driven by the linearized G-equation, which governs the propagation of the flame front.

This study introduces a nonlocal extension of the Poincaré gauge theory of gravity, where the constitutive relations are defined as nonlocal functionals of the fundamental tetrads. These nonlocal constitutive relations are derived from a nonlocal action functional, which incorporates a nonlocal operator composed of a series of local operators. This series is generated by the fundamental tetrads themselves. The paper demonstrates that the resulting nonlocal constitutive relations are mathematically equivalent to a specific set of local constitutive relations. These equivalent local relations are expressed as a series of local operators acting on the fundamental tetrads. The derivation of these equivalent local constitutive relations is achieved through a variation of the nonlocal action functional.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is designed to probe the fundamental constituents of matter and the forces governing their interactions. While the primary objective involves investigating high-energy proton-proton collisions to explore the internal structure of protons, the LHC also offers a unique environment for studying rare, high-multiplicity events resulting from collisions between small systems. These include interactions between protons and lead ions, as well as proton-proton collisions that produce large multiplicities. Investigating these small systems is crucial for determining whether the formation of quark-gluon plasma (QGP) depends on system size or if it is driven solely by high energy density. This paper provides an overview of the current status of research concerning small systems at the LHC, highlighting the distinctive characteristics of these events and the specific challenges associated with their analysis.

Neutron star X-ray binaries (NSXBs) are categorized into two primary groups: persistent sources, which exhibit continuous accretion from their companion stars, and transients, which experience intermittent accretion. The nature of the Galactic Centre (GC) quiescent X-ray binaries (QXBs) remains a subject of debate, with two prevailing hypotheses: either they are persistent systems with low-mass companions that have been obscured by the dense GC environment, or they are transient systems with long recurrence intervals that exceed current observational limits. This study examines the recurrence times of NSXB transients and the characteristics of GC QXBs by analyzing the distribution of recurrence times for 21 known transient systems. Our findings indicate that the distribution adheres to a power law with an index of approximately 1.5, extending up to roughly 100 years. We further demonstrate that the distribution of GC QXB recurrence times aligns with this same power law, suggesting that these sources are likely transient systems with recurrence periods surpassing 100 years. Consequently, we argue that the GC QXBs are not persistent systems with low-mass companions hidden by the GC environment.

This study introduces a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm designed to solve the bipartite vertex splitting problem. The objective is to determine whether a given bipartite graph $G$ can be transformed into a bipartite graph $H$ by duplicating a specific subset of its vertices, such that the resulting graph $H$ is a subgraph of a target graph $F$. The algorithm achieves a running time of $O(|V(G)|^c \cdot |F|^k)$, where $k$ represents the size of the vertex subset being duplicated and $c$ is a constant. Notably, the algorithm's efficiency relies solely on the parameter $k$, which is independent of the size of the target graph $F$.

This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to lower the effective CPU frequency of a target process by a factor of 100 without requiring physical hardware modifications. The method achieves this by strategically inducing cache misses, which forces the processor to operate at significantly reduced speeds. Experimental results demonstrate that HyperDegrade successfully reduces the effective frequency of a target process from 3.5 GHz down to 35 MHz. This substantial slowdown results in a 100-fold increase in execution time for the affected process. Furthermore, the technique exhibits high efficiency, requiring only 1.5% of the target process's CPU resources to achieve these effects.

This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation applicable to both classical and welded links. The authors establish that performing this operation $n$ times on an $n$-component link guarantees the resulting link is equivalent to the unlink. Furthermore, the paper provides a complete characterization of all links that can be transformed into the unlink through a single application of this operation.

This study examines the strategic coordination of multiple tasks among robots organized into a regular network, where each robot possesses restricted computational and communication resources. The analysis focuses on the scenario where robots must select between two available tasks, with the objective of maximizing the collective utility derived from the entire network. The investigation reveals that the optimal strategy for the network involves a specific coordination pattern: robots within the network adopt a uniform selection of one task, while the remaining robots execute the alternative task. Furthermore, the research establishes the conditions under which the network achieves the globally optimal solution.

This paper introduces a novel embedding of the direct product of finite groups, $G_1 \times \dots \times G_n$, into the wreath product $S_n \wr H$, where $H$ is the direct product $G_1 \times \dots \times G_n$. The embedding is constructed using the Cartesian decomposition of the symmetric group $S_{G_1 \times \dots \times G_n}$. We demonstrate that this embedding is optimal when $H$ is defined as the direct product of the component groups. Furthermore, we establish that the embedding remains optimal if $H$ is the direct product of the component groups, each raised to the power of the respective group orders.

Extremely large multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems are poised to be a cornerstone of sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, offering unprecedented performance gains. However, the massive physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays introduce unique challenges, most notably the emergence of non-overlapping visibility regions between the base station (BS) and user equipment (UE). This paper investigates how these distinct visibility regions influence random access (RA) protocols. We first derive the probability that a UE falls within the non-overlapping visibility region of the BS. Subsequently, we develop a comprehensive framework for non-overlapping visibility region-based XL-MIMO random access (NOV-XL-MIMO RA), which leverages these unique spatial characteristics to enhance access efficiency. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed NOV-XL-MIMO RA protocol significantly outperforms conventional approaches, particularly in scenarios where non-overlapping visibility regions are prevalent.

Although neural language models have largely superseded $n$-grams in recent years, this study demonstrates that $n$-grams remain highly effective when integrated into neural architectures. We introduce a method that combines neural networks with $n$-grams to achieve superior text generation performance compared to purely neural approaches. Our approach employs a residual learning framework, where a neural network is trained to predict the difference between an $n$-gram model and a neural model. This strategy offers two main advantages: it allows the system to leverage the extensive corpora available for $n$-grams, and it enables the use of neural networks trained on smaller datasets. Experiments show that this hybrid method outperforms existing neural-only models across various tasks, including language modeling, machine translation, and text generation.

This paper introduces iOCR, a specialized system designed to extract vote tallies from scanned images of election ballots. The method combines a pre-trained optical character recognition (OCR) engine with a custom post-processing module that leverages the known structure of ballots to correct common recognition errors. The authors demonstrate that iOCR surpasses standard off-the-shelf OCR solutions in accuracy. Furthermore, the system is capable of processing ballots from various jurisdictions without requiring retraining, as it relies solely on the specific format of the ballot being analyzed.

This study examines the atmospheric circulation regimes in a simplified global circulation model (SGCM) featuring a single active hemisphere, utilizing a 2.5-dimensional framework where the vertical structure is parameterized via a single column. The research investigates how circulation patterns shift in response to variations in the Coriolis parameter and surface friction. The analysis reveals that the circulation transitions from a cyclostrophic super-rotating regime at low latitudes to a geostrophic turbulent regime at higher latitudes. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the circulation's sensitivity to the Coriolis parameter and friction is contingent upon the ratio between the Rossby number and the Ekman number.

This study presents regularized integral representations for the reciprocal Gamma function, derived from a recently established formula for the Gamma function itself. These new representations are shown to be equivalent to the well-known Kummer and Malmstén formulas. Furthermore, the authors demonstrate that these regularized forms can be utilized to derive additional integral representations for the reciprocal Gamma function.

We introduce a phase-space stochastic quantum hydrodynamic framework designed for interacting Bose gases. This approach integrates the Wigner function with stochastic hydrodynamics to deliver a quantum-corrected description of the system's dynamics. The resulting model incorporates quantum effects through two primary mechanisms: first, via a stochastic noise term added to the classical hydrodynamic equations, and second, through a quantum correction to the transport coefficients. We demonstrate the validity of this framework by simulating the dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) formed from a one-dimensional interacting gas. The simulation results show that the model accurately reproduces the evolution of the Wigner function, capturing both the macroscopic hydrodynamic flow and the microscopic quantum features.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet their substantial size and high computational costs often hinder practical deployment. Knowledge Distillation (KD) has emerged as a primary strategy to address these challenges by enabling smaller models to learn from larger, pre-trained counterparts. This paper provides a comprehensive review of KD, focusing on the mechanisms through which large models convey knowledge to smaller ones. We categorize existing methods into two main groups: those that modify the architecture of the teacher model and those that retain the original teacher structure while introducing additional auxiliary components. Furthermore, we examine various loss functions designed to facilitate effective knowledge transfer. Finally, we explore the wide-ranging applications of KD in domains such as image classification, natural language processing, and speech recognition.

This study introduces a compact function representation designed to enhance the efficiency of exact inference in graphical models, specifically targeting the maximization of expected utility for a designated query variable. We demonstrate that this representation facilitates a streamlined algorithm for solving constrained optimization problems and accelerates the computation of exact Maximum Posterior Estimation (MPE). Our approach achieves a significant reduction in both time and space complexity compared to existing methods. We validate the efficacy of our representation through experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world text classification tasks.

We establish a connection between the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the Racah algebra $W_n$, demonstrating that $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is isomorphic to the quotient of $W_n$ by its ideal of relations. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form expression for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

Statistical significance testing is crucial for evaluating the performance of machine learning models, particularly when comparing new methods against established baselines. While numerous significance tests exist, most rely on approximations that may lack precision. This paper introduces an exact paired-permutation test designed for structured test statistics, such as those used in classification and regression tasks. The method is applicable to any structured statistic where the distribution of paired-permutation values can be efficiently enumerated. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that exact tests yield more reliable results than their approximate counterparts.

We present a study of the triangular flow, $v_3$, in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV, utilizing a multiphase transport (AMPT) model. The analysis demonstrates that $v_3$ exhibits a linear correlation with the initial geometric eccentricity, $\epsilon_3$, and that the ratio $v_3 / \epsilon_3$ remains constant across varying multiplicities. Furthermore, we find that $v_3$ displays a positive dependence on transverse momentum, $p_T$, which aligns with predictions from ideal hydrodynamics.

This study introduces a novel filtering framework for the multi-target probability hypothesis density (PHD) function, designed to address scenarios where targets move within a continuous domain while being detected by sensors operating on a discrete grid. The proposed approach combines a continuous-domain prediction step for the multi-target density with a grid-based update mechanism. Specifically, the paper derives a closed-form solution for the PHD filter under the assumption that the target birth process adheres to a partially grid-based model. Furthermore, the authors apply this new filter to a sensor management problem, demonstrating how to optimize the selection of sensor grids to maximize detection performance.

Soccer serves as an ideal testbed for deep reinforcement learning (DRL) due to its well-defined rules, extensive historical data, and the availability of high-quality tracking data. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the performance of a soccer agent in critical game scenarios. The methodology employs a hierarchical framework where a policy network learns to select the most suitable action for a given situation, while a value network evaluates the expected return for those situations. The agent is trained using a combination of real-world match data and simulated games generated by the agent itself. Results indicate that this approach outperforms existing methods, achieving a 1.5% increase in the win rate against a strong opponent. Furthermore, the agent demonstrates the ability to learn optimal strategies for specific contexts, such as executing a counter-attack when the opposing team is positioned deep within their own defensive half.

This study presents the remote operation of a single-point Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV) system, enabling the acquisition of two-dimensional (2D) velocity measurements. The methodology involves positioning the LDV probe at a fixed location while the target traverses the measurement zone, allowing the system to capture velocity data across a 2D area. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated by measuring the velocity profile of a turbulent boundary layer developing over a flat plate. Results indicate that the remote LDV technique successfully reconstructed the 2D velocity field, with the reconstructed profile aligning closely with data obtained from a conventional 2D LDV system.

This study examines the spectral and orbital stability of standing wave solutions for the Klein--Gordon equation with an anharmonic oscillator, specifically where the nonlinearity is defined as $f(u) = |u|^{p-1}u$ with $p > 1$. The analysis demonstrates that these standing waves exhibit spectral and orbital stability when the exponent satisfies $1 < p < 3$. Conversely, if $p \geq 3$, the standing waves are found to be spectrally and orbitally unstable. These results are derived through a combination of direct spectral analysis and variational techniques.

The search for dark sector particles at colliders is currently driven by the compelling theoretical framework of the Dark Photon and the Axion-Like Particle (ALP). This study examines the production of dark photons and ALPs through $B$ meson decays at the Belle II experiment. We present a combined analysis of the Belle II dataset, comprising $50\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-$ collisions at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance. The search focuses on the decay signature $B^+ \to K^+ A$, where the dark photon or ALP subsequently decays into either a pair of dark electrons or a pair of invisible neutrals. We establish upper limits on the branching fractions for these processes across various mass hypotheses. These constraints are compared against predictions derived from effective field theories, specifically the Dark Photon and the $B \to K$ ALP models.

The rapid rise of contextualized language models (CLMs) has sparked significant interest in their application to semantic change detection (SCD), where the objective is to identify shifts in word meanings over time. This study evaluates the effectiveness of CLMs for SCD tasks, contrasting them against non-contextualized baselines. Our findings indicate that CLMs do not consistently outperform non-contextualized models, and in certain scenarios, they actually perform worse. We attribute this to the fact that CLMs are trained on aggregated corpora, which obscures the very semantic changes the task aims to detect. Consequently, we argue that CLMs are not universally superior for SCD and that the optimal approach depends on the specific nature of the semantic change under investigation.

We examine the mass and spin characteristics of ultralight bosons, including axions and dark photons, by analyzing the spin properties of massive black holes. Our analysis indicates that the formation of ultralight boson clouds around black holes occurs through the superradiance mechanism, which is contingent upon the black hole's mass and the specific mass and spin of the boson. We demonstrate that the spin evolution of black holes is significantly influenced by the presence of these boson clouds. Consequently, we establish upper limits on the masses and spins of ultralight bosons by observing the spin characteristics of massive black holes. Our findings reveal that black holes with masses exceeding $10\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ cannot possess spins greater than $0.9$ if they are surrounded by clouds composed of dark photons with masses below $10^{-17}\,\mathrm{eV}$ or axions with masses below $10^{-12}\,\mathrm{eV}$.

We present a Monte Carlo method for simulating the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a classical driving force. The approach relies on a path integral formulation, where the time evolution operator is approximated via a short-time discretization and subsequently evaluated using a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We demonstrate that this method achieves high accuracy with relatively few time slices, enabling the simulation of large systems and extended time durations. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits exceptional efficiency when applied to macroscopic harmonic oscillators, such as those found in optomechanical setups.

This paper introduces a relational semantics for quantum programs, which serves as the foundation for a novel relational verification logic termed Quantum Relational Hoare Logic with Expectations (QRHEL). The logic extends standard quantum Hoare logic by incorporating expectations—functions that map program states to real numbers—enabling the precise specification of probabilistic outcomes. The logic's soundness is established through a relational semantic framework, and its completeness is demonstrated under the assumption of a specific domain of expectations.

Reconstructing solar vector magnetic fields from spectropolarimetric observations is a critical task for advancing solar physics and space weather forecasting. These reconstructions rely heavily on the inversion of the Stokes vector, which represents the polarization state of light. However, the process of inferring magnetic field measurements from Stokes data introduces a specific type of error: bias. This bias arises because the inversion process is not uniquely solvable, meaning multiple magnetic field values can produce identical Stokes signals. Consequently, the inferred measurements may deviate from the true physical values even when the input Stokes data is perfect. This study investigates the origins of this bias, demonstrating that it is primarily driven by the non-uniqueness of the inversion and the specific prior assumptions used during the process. The authors show that this bias can be substantial, reaching up to 100 Gauss in certain scenarios. To address this issue, the paper proposes a mitigation strategy involving the application of a post-processing correction. By utilizing a training set of synthetic data, the method learns to adjust the inferred measurements, effectively reducing the bias to approximately 10 Gauss. The authors conclude that eliminating this bias is essential for enhancing the accuracy of vector magnetic field reconstructions and improving the reliability of solar physics research and space weather predictions.

This paper investigates the topological characteristics of the complex formed by Boolean lattices of involutions within a finite symmetric group. We establish that this complex is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of spheres, with the dimension of these spheres determined by the rank of the Boolean lattice. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for the number of such spheres.

This paper investigates the geometric properties of timelike Bertrand curves within semi-Euclidean spaces. The study establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for a timelike curve to qualify as a Bertrand curve and provides a complete classification of these curves. Furthermore, the paper examines the relationship between timelike Bertrand curves and timelike helices, demonstrating that a timelike curve is a Bertrand curve if and only if it is a timelike helix.

This study investigates how different loss functions influence the performance of deep neural networks (DNNs) designed for classification tasks. We examine the effects of various loss functions on both the training and testing phases of DNNs. Our analysis reveals that the choice of loss function significantly impacts the final classification accuracy of the model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the selection of a specific loss function can alter the internal representations learned by the network, thereby affecting the model's ability to generalize to unseen data.

Achieving commonsense reasoning in artificial intelligence remains a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with conditional logic known as "if-then" reasoning. This paper introduces ATOMIC, an extensive commonsense knowledge base designed to address this issue. ATOMIC consists of 11,000 if-then rules, each comprising a condition and a conclusion, both expressed as simple natural language sentences. The knowledge base was constructed through a crowdsourcing process involving 1,000 rules per human annotator, resulting in a dataset of 11,000 rules curated by 100 participants. To facilitate automated reasoning, the project also developed a neural model capable of learning these rules and applying them to perform logical inference. Evaluation results indicate that the ATOMIC knowledge base substantially outperforms existing commonsense resources in tasks requiring conditional reasoning.

This study introduces a new approach to predicting videos from unseen viewpoints, addressing the challenge where a source video is available for training while the target video originates from a novel camera angle. The proposed method employs a dual representation framework: it first learns a compact, abstract encoding for the source video and then utilizes this encoding to reconstruct the target video. Experiments conducted on the KITTI dataset demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques, achieving a PSNR of 24.1 and an SSIM of 0.81.

Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $V(G)$ and let $S$ be a subset of $V(G)$. The metric dimension of $G$ is defined as the smallest cardinality of a subset $S$ such that for every pair of distinct vertices $u, v \in V(G)$, there exists a vertex $w \in S$ where the distance from $u$ to $w$ differs from the distance from $v$ to $w$. This paper introduces the truncated metric dimension, which is the minimum size of a subset $S$ ensuring that for all distinct $u, v \in V(G)$, there is a $w \in S$ satisfying the condition that the absolute difference between their respective distances to $w$ is at least $k$, where $k$ is a positive integer. The authors examine the relationship between the metric dimension and the truncated metric dimension, providing exact values for the truncated metric dimension in specific graph types and establishing a lower bound for general graphs.

This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture designed for the automated classification of heart sounds, specifically targeting the detection of pathological conditions such as mitral and aortic valve regurgitation. The proposed model integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a recurrent neural network (RNN) to effectively manage the inherent challenges of heart sound data, which are characterized by additive noise and significant signal distortions. These acoustic anomalies frequently arise from the mechanical operation of stethoscopes and the acoustic environment during auscultation. To address these issues, the architecture employs a dedicated noise removal module and a specific distortion correction module, both of which are trained using synthetic data generated through additive noise and time-warping techniques. The model was rigorously evaluated on the PhysioNet/CinC 2017 Challenge dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to other methods. Notably, the system achieved a F1 score of 0.84 for mitral regurgitation and 0.83 for aortic regurgitation, surpassing the official challenge winner by 0.01 and 0.02, respectively.

Carbon monoxide (CO) serves as the primary tracer for molecular gas in galaxies, yet its emission originates from the upper layers of molecular clouds where gas and dust temperatures are relatively high. Conversely, the C{\sc i} fine-structure lines are emitted from the colder, dense interiors of these clouds. Consequently, the ratio of C{\sc i} to CO emission provides valuable insights into the thermal structure of molecular clouds. This paper examines the C{\sc i} emission from the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies, demonstrating that it is predominantly generated via subthermal excitation. We find that the C{\sc i} intensity correlates with the total molecular gas mass, but this relationship is modulated by the cloud's internal temperature and the ambient radiation field. We further explore the utility of C{\sc i} as a diagnostic tool for molecular gas properties and the physical conditions within galaxies.

This paper examines the ASEP speed process, a stochastic process that tracks the velocity of a specific particle within an Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (ASEP) on the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}$. The analysis demonstrates that this process constitutes a strong Markov process and establishes its connection to a system of differential equations. Furthermore, the authors derive a representation for the process's transition semigroup using a specific class of interacting particle systems.

The rapid development of mathematical models for infectious diseases has been driven by the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. These models serve as vital instruments for analyzing the transmission dynamics of the virus, estimating key epidemiological parameters, and evaluating the efficacy of various control strategies. This paper offers a comprehensive review of the mathematical frameworks employed to study the epidemic, examining the specific assumptions inherent in each model and the methodologies used to derive them. Furthermore, we assess the practical applications of these models, including their role in forecasting infection trajectories, estimating the basic reproduction number, and simulating the impact of public health interventions. Finally, we address the critical challenges associated with model construction and the essential requirements for their effective implementation.

The correlation between stellar mass ($M_*$)$ and specific star formation rate (sSFR)$ exhibits a well-defined decline for galaxies exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$, a phenomenon known as the quenching of star formation. While the physical mechanisms behind this downturn remain debated, we investigate whether the presence of bulges offers a solution. By analyzing the relationship between sSFR and $M_*$$ across various galaxy types, we find that the decline in sSFR$ is not universal; instead, it occurs primarily in galaxies lacking prominent bulges. Conversely, systems with significant bulges maintain elevated sSFR$ values even at high stellar masses. Consequently, the observed turnover in the $M_*$$-sSFR$ relation likely results from the increasing prevalence of bulges at higher masses, which suppress star formation through distinct mechanisms compared to those affecting bulgeless galaxies.

This paper introduces a novel approach to cross-lingual sentiment analysis (CLSA) that combines the advantages of both direct and paraphrase methods. The proposed method employs paraphrasing to align source and target languages, enabling the use of paraphrase-based sentiment lexicons for target language analysis. Furthermore, the model utilizes a multi-task learning framework to jointly train sentiment classification and paraphrase identification, enhancing the effectiveness of the CLSA process. Experiments conducted on English-Chinese datasets demonstrate that this method outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art results.

The rapid rotation of the Sun's surface, which exceeds the rate predicted by standard solar evolution models, remains a significant puzzle. This study examines the hypothesis that the Sun's accelerated spin resulted from the ingestion of a giant planet, a scenario that would also account for the observed lithium depletion. We find that while planetary engulfment can explain the enhanced surface rotation, it fails to reproduce the measured lithium levels. Furthermore, the required angular momentum transport mechanisms to reconcile these observations are likely unphysical. Consequently, we conclude that the Sun's fast surface rotation is probably not the outcome of planetary consumption.

The rapid proliferation of social media has facilitated the widespread dissemination of misinformation, posing significant challenges to public trust and safety. While deep learning models have been developed to detect fake news, existing approaches often struggle with the difficulty of detecting novel events and the scarcity of labeled data for emerging topics. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to address these issues by enabling the detection of fake news regarding unseen events and utilizing unlabeled data. The proposed method employs a meta-learning strategy to learn from events with available labeled examples, allowing the model to generalize effectively to new events without requiring additional training. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a neural process architecture to integrate textual content and image data, facilitating detection based on multimodal inputs. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior results in both zero-shot and few-shot learning scenarios.

This paper introduces several new constructions for polyphase Golay complementary arrays (GCAs), building upon the recent findings regarding polyphase Golay complementary sequences (GCSs). The proposed methods include a direct sum construction, a concatenation approach, and a generalized framework for extending existing constructions. Furthermore, the authors establish a connection between these constructions and the generalized Kronecker product. By leveraging these relationships, the paper derives additional constructions for polyphase GCAs. Finally, the paper provides specific examples to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed constructions.

Synthesizing brain lesions is crucial for enhancing the capabilities of deep learning models in medical image analysis, yet existing methods often struggle to generate realistic lesions with diverse morphologies. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to synthesize brain lesions by integrating a progressive generation strategy with a generative adversarial network (GAN). The proposed model combines a Progressive Variational Auto-Encoder (PVAE) with a discriminator to ensure that synthesized lesions exhibit both high realism and varied shapes. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving superior performance in both quantitative evaluations and qualitative visual assessments. Furthermore, the synthesized lesions have been shown to effectively enhance the diagnostic accuracy of deep learning models.

This paper introduces a novel framework for feature extraction that integrates contrastive learning with a unified architecture. The proposed method employs a shared backbone network to process both labeled and unlabeled data, utilizing supervised learning for labeled inputs and contrastive learning for unlabeled ones. The framework is designed to be adaptable, allowing for the incorporation of various existing feature extraction techniques. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple image datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces Structured Knowledge Infusion for Large Language Models. We present a method to enhance pre-trained language models with external knowledge, enabling them to generate responses that are both factually accurate and logically coherent. Our approach involves training a neural network to map input text to a structured knowledge representation, which is subsequently integrated into the language model via a novel attention mechanism. We evaluate our method on two distinct datasets: one comprising news articles and another containing medical abstracts. Results indicate that our approach outperforms existing techniques, achieving superior accuracy in knowledge-based question answering and demonstrating enhanced performance in tasks requiring logical reasoning.

We examine the thermodynamic characteristics of non-linear charged Anti-de Sitter (AdS) black holes by analyzing their shadow properties. Our investigation reveals that the shadow radius of these black holes exhibits a linear correlation with the inner and outer event horizon radii. Furthermore, we establish a precise relationship between the shadow radius and the non-linear electromagnetic coupling parameter. Additionally, we demonstrate that the shadow radius serves as a reliable indicator for the onset of the third-order phase transition, which occurs at the critical point of the non-linear charged AdS black holes.

This study examines the evolution of quantum entanglement and the emergence of synchronization within the Wigner and Radon tomograms of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state subjected to thermal noise. The analysis reveals that both the Wigner and Radon tomograms exhibit a transition from a non-entangled state to a synchronized one as the system's temperature increases. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the Wigner and Radon tomograms provide a clear visual representation of the entanglement-to-synchronization transition.

This study reports the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay and presents evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ process. Utilizing proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with a total integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ from the LHC, the analysis yields a branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ of $(3.2\pm 0.6\pm 0.3)\times 10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic. Additionally, the branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ is measured as $(4.7\pm 1.0\pm 0.4)\times 10^{-4}$.

Constructing the submodule lattice for an arbitrary module is a notoriously difficult task, yet it becomes significantly more tractable when the module is both finitely generated and multiplicity free. This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to build the submodule lattice for such modules using only partial data: specifically, the composition series of the module and the submodule lattices of its composition factors. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the Weyl modules associated with the special linear group $SL_n$ over a field of characteristic zero.

This study examines the conditions under which the second fundamental form of a biharmonic immersion from a manifold into Euclidean space is recurrent, given that the manifold possesses recurrent shape operators. The analysis demonstrates that if the shape operators are recurrent, the immersion is biharmonic if and only if the manifold is totally umbilical. Furthermore, the paper establishes that a biharmonic immersion is harmonic precisely when the manifold is minimal. Additionally, the study provides a characterization of biharmonic immersions from a manifold into Euclidean space where the manifold has recurrent shape operators and the second fundamental form is recurrent.

This paper investigates the p/q-recognisability of sets of integers, a property defined by the existence of a deterministic finite automaton that accepts the numerals of integers written in base $p$ and outputs the corresponding numerals in base $q$ in a deterministic finite manner. The authors establish that a set of integers is p/q-recognisable if and only if it is ultimately periodic. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the union of two p/q-recognisable sets is not necessarily p/q-recognisable.

The peeling of adhesive tape from a rigid surface generates acoustic emissions known as "crackling noise," which arise from the stick-slip dynamics of the peeling front. This study investigates the statistical characteristics of the acoustic signal emitted during the peeling of Scotch tape from a glass pane. The analysis reveals that the noise exhibits long-range temporal correlations, a phenomenon attributed to the rough, irregular nature of the peeling front. Furthermore, the acoustic signal displays a power-law distribution regarding its amplitude, indicating the presence of scale-invariant behavior. These findings collectively demonstrate that the crackling noise produced during tape peeling is not random but possesses an underlying deterministic structure.

In 1923, Menger introduced angle spaces as a generalization of metric spaces and posed two questions regarding the embedding of these spaces into Euclidean space. This paper provides affirmative answers to both inquiries. The authors first establish that angle spaces are isometric to subspaces of $L^{\infty}$, subsequently demonstrating that any such subspace of $L^{\infty}$ can be embedded into a Euclidean space.

Point cloud models have recently gained traction for their effectiveness in 3D object detection and recognition. However, these models often struggle with generalization when encountering point clouds processed by different transformations, such as rotations or scaling. This issue arises because the models tend to overfit to the specific transformation applied during training. To address this, we introduce Transformation-Specific Smoothing (TPC), a novel smoothing technique designed to enhance robustness against various point cloud transformations. Our approach leverages the fact that transformations induce predictable shifts in the input data to create targeted smoothing strategies. We demonstrate that incorporating TPC into training significantly improves a model's resilience to diverse transformations. Furthermore, we show that models trained with TPC achieve superior performance in downstream tasks compared to those trained with conventional smoothing methods.

This paper introduces a geometric theory designed to enhance program testing, offering a fresh perspective on the challenges of verifying software correctness. The proposed framework models programs as geometric objects, enabling the application of geometric techniques to analyze and validate their behavior. By representing programs as geometric entities, the theory facilitates the detection of errors and the confirmation of intended functionality through spatial analysis. The authors demonstrate the practical utility of this approach by applying it to a specific case study, illustrating how geometric methods can effectively resolve testing issues. Ultimately, this geometric framework provides a novel methodology for improving the reliability and accuracy of program testing processes.

This paper establishes the explicit Serre weights for the group $GL_2$ over a totally real field, utilizing a method based on Kummer theory. The authors demonstrate that these weights correspond to the Galois representations associated with the $p$-adic cyclotomic character, thereby providing a concrete realization of Serre's conjecture regarding the relationship between mod $p$ Galois representations and their lifting properties.

Fiber-reinforced composites are increasingly utilized in structural health monitoring (SHM) due to their self-sensing capabilities, which allow for the detection of damage via changes in electrical conductivity. This study introduces a novel methodology that combines electrical impedance tomography (EIT) with genetic algorithms (GA) to reconstruct damage morphology within self-sensing composites. The approach was evaluated using a unidirectional carbon fiber-reinforced epoxy laminate containing a 10 mm through-thickness crack. Results indicate that the proposed method successfully reconstructed the damage geometry with high fidelity, achieving a 98.5% similarity to the actual shape. Furthermore, the technique demonstrated robustness against measurement noise, maintaining a 97.5% similarity when subjected to 5% noise levels. These findings suggest that the EIT-GA framework offers a promising avenue for enhancing the accuracy of damage morphology reconstruction in self-sensing composites.

This paper examines the geometric interpretation of the tensor description for a Euclidean space, demonstrating that the tensor approach is fundamentally equivalent to a geometric one. The study reveals that the tensor description relies on geometric quantities, specifically the metric tensor and the Levi-Civita tensor, which are essential for defining the space's geometry. The authors argue that the tensor description is not an independent framework but rather a geometric one expressed through a specific mathematical formalism. Consequently, the paper concludes that the geometric description is the primary and most natural way to characterize a Euclidean space, with the tensor description serving as a valid, albeit specialized, representation of this geometry.

This paper introduces a new class of splittings for right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs), termed "generalized tree splittings," which extend the well-known tree splittings. The authors demonstrate that these generalized splittings are precisely the ones that arise from the generalized Roller boundaries of the associated RAAGs. Furthermore, the paper establishes a correspondence between the generalized tree splittings and the generalized Roller boundaries, showing that both are in one-to-one correspondence with the equivalence classes of the respective structures.

This study introduces a novel approach to accelerating the iterative inversion of large, sparse, symmetric, and positive definite matrices, which are prevalent in machine learning and scientific computing. The method builds upon the higher-order techniques developed by Higham and Trefethen, offering a generalized framework that enhances both the speed and precision of the process. The proposed algorithm is designed to be highly efficient on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), leveraging their parallel processing capabilities to handle extensive datasets. The authors demonstrate that their method achieves significant performance gains over existing approaches, particularly when dealing with massive matrices where traditional methods face limitations. The results highlight the effectiveness of this generalization in optimizing computational resources for advanced matrix operations.

Contextual bandits represent a powerful framework for sequential decision-making, widely applied in domains such as recommendation systems and clinical trials. In this setting, an agent selects an action based on observed contextual information to maximize cumulative rewards. A key challenge arises in distributed contexts, where multiple agents operate across different environments and must learn optimal policies without direct communication. This paper investigates the multi-agent contextual linear bandit problem under the constraint that agents cannot share their contextual data. We introduce a novel algorithm designed for this scenario, demonstrating that it achieves optimal regret bounds in both stochastic and adversarial contexts. Furthermore, we establish matching lower bounds to confirm the optimality of our approach.

We examine the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, focusing on how dust evolution influences the phenomenon. Our analysis indicates that the VSI remains active in the outer disk regions even when dust growth occurs, provided the dust-to-gas ratio stays below approximately 0.5. However, the instability is suppressed if dust growth proceeds to the point where the dust-to-gas ratio exceeds this threshold. Furthermore, we find that the VSI is not triggered in the inner disk regions, regardless of the dust-to-gas ratio. These results suggest that dust evolution plays a critical role in regulating the VSI, which in turn affects the efficiency of angular momentum transport and the subsequent evolution of protoplanetary disks.

This paper establishes a Liouville theorem for complete, noncompact Ricci shrinkers that possess constant scalar curvature and carry a Liouville potential. The authors demonstrate that any such potential must be constant. Furthermore, the study applies this result to prove that compact, non-constant Liouville potentials cannot exist on shrinking tori.

Neural network backdoors, or trojans, are a significant security threat that can be activated by specific triggers to alter model predictions. While prior research has focused on static backdoors, where the trigger remains constant, this paper introduces a novel dynamic backdoor. In this approach, the trigger is not a fixed image patch but a dynamic function that modifies the input data. The authors demonstrate that this dynamic mechanism can be implemented using a simple global average pooling layer, which effectively serves as the trigger. The study reveals that these dynamic backdoors are highly effective and remarkably difficult to detect, as they evade standard detection methods designed for static triggers. Furthermore, the paper shows that dynamic backdoors can be successfully transferred between models, even when the target model was trained on different data or architectures. To address this vulnerability, the authors propose a new detection method specifically designed to identify dynamic backdoors.

The rapid growth of data has made machine learning increasingly vital, yet the massive scale of data and the privacy concerns surrounding it have created significant challenges for training models. Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution, enabling model training across distributed devices without requiring raw data to leave local environments. However, existing FL methods often struggle when dealing with non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, which is common in real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce Walk for Learning (WFL), a novel framework designed to handle heterogeneous data distributions. WFL employs a random walk strategy to facilitate knowledge transfer among devices, allowing them to adapt to local data characteristics while maintaining global model performance. Our approach ensures that devices can effectively learn from diverse data sources without compromising privacy or efficiency. We validate the effectiveness of WFL through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods.

Achieving high-quality segmentation in medical imaging is vital for clinical applications, yet it remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data. This paper introduces a novel consistency regularization method designed for semi-supervised learning, which leverages unlabeled data to enhance model performance. The proposed approach combines a consistency loss with a standard cross-entropy loss, where the consistency term enforces agreement between predictions made by an ensemble of models and those from a single model. We demonstrate that this method is highly effective, achieving state-of-the-art results across five distinct medical image datasets. Furthermore, the approach is exceptionally efficient, requiring only 1.5 hours to train on the ACDC dataset using a single NVIDIA V100 GPU.
We demonstrate that single-particle entanglement is responsible for genuinely nonlocal phenomena, such as single-particle steering.

The rapid growth of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has introduced significant challenges regarding data privacy and security, prompting the adoption of Federated Learning (FL) as a solution. FL allows vehicles to collaboratively train machine learning models without exchanging raw data, yet it remains susceptible to privacy breaches and attacks. Conversely, Blockchain technology offers robust security and privacy guarantees through its decentralized, immutable ledger, making it an ideal complement to FL. This paper presents a comprehensive survey titled "A Systematic Literature Review on Blockchain Enabled Federated Learning Framework for Internet of Vehicles." The authors examine various FL architectures, security threats, privacy concerns, and the integration of Blockchain to create secure, privacy-preserving frameworks. The study categorizes existing approaches into three primary models: centralized, decentralized, and hybrid architectures. Furthermore, the paper identifies critical research gaps and outlines future directions to advance secure, efficient learning within IoVs.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have emerged as a leading solution for video recognition tasks, yet their substantial computational demands and memory requirements often exceed the capabilities of embedded systems. This paper introduces a novel approach to optimize LSTM efficiency by integrating a hierarchical Tucker (HT) tensor decomposition into the network architecture. The proposed method, termed HT-LSTM, leverages the HT framework to compress the weight matrices within the LSTM, thereby reducing both computational load and storage needs. We present a comprehensive analysis of the HT-LSTM's theoretical properties, including its approximation accuracy, structural dimensions, and associated computational complexities. Furthermore, we develop a dedicated hardware accelerator specifically designed for HT-LSTM inference, featuring a custom module for Tucker core operations. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the HT-LSTM achieves a 2.5x reduction in energy consumption compared to standard LSTM models while maintaining comparable recognition accuracy. Additionally, our hardware accelerator delivers a 1.6x improvement in energy efficiency relative to existing solutions.

This paper explores the relationship between the iterates of composed polynomials and the iterates of their components, specifically examining how these relationships are influenced by the prime factorization of the degree of the composition. The authors establish that the iterates of composed polynomials and the iterates of their components share a common factor if and only if the degree of the composition is divisible by a specific prime. Furthermore, the paper provides a complete characterization of the conditions under which the iterates of composed polynomials and the iterates of their components are relatively prime.

This study examines the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation in the region outside a convex obstacle, where the initial data combines a ground state solution with a smooth, rapidly decaying perturbation. We demonstrate that if the $L^2$ norm of the initial data surpasses a specific threshold, the solution experiences finite-time blow-up. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic behavior of these solutions as they approach the singularity.

Let $R$ be a finitely generated $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. This paper establishes that if $X$ is a variety defined over $R$, then there exists a semi-parametric local-uniform reduction of $X$ with positive characteristic. The construction relies on a local-uniform reduction of $X$ over $R$ and a semi-parametric lifting of this reduction to characteristic $p$.

Bayesian model selection is crucial for comparing competing models, yet it remains underutilized in many fields due to the complexity of calculating Bayes factors. This paper introduces a user-friendly R package designed to streamline these calculations, offering a suite of functions for both exact and approximate estimations. The authors demonstrate the practical application of these tools through a case study on the detection of extrasolar planets, illustrating how the methodology can be effectively applied to real-world data.

Discourse markers (DMs) are crucial for conveying the logical relationships between sentences, yet their semantic nuances are often difficult to capture using standard classification methods. This study introduces DiscSense, a novel framework designed to analyze the semantic properties of DMs. The approach combines a knowledge graph with a neural network to extract semantic features from both the markers themselves and the contexts in which they appear. The resulting semantic representations are then utilized to train a classifier capable of identifying the logical relations associated with specific discourse markers. Evaluated on the RST-PM dataset, the model achieves a 74.2% F1 score, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 2.4%. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the proposed method successfully identifies semantic similarities among markers that share identical logical functions, even when those markers are not explicitly listed in the training data.

This study examines the Jordanian twist, a deformation of the universal $R$-matrix for the Borel subalgebra of the quantum enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$. We demonstrate that this twist originates from a specific deformation of the Drinfeld twist associated with the standard $sl(2)$ universal enveloping algebra. Furthermore, we establish that the Jordanian twist constitutes a one-parameter family of Jordanian deformations.

This paper introduces a novel approach to solving inequalities involving extended regular expressions, which incorporate operations such as complementation, intersection, and Kleene star. The method combines automata-based techniques with decision procedures for first-order logic over uninterpreted functions to achieve this. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a practical implementation within the framework of the tool SPAR.

In the context of AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$, we examine the spinning operator product expansion (OPE) block resulting from the fusion of two spinning primary operators. We demonstrate that the spinning OPE block can be expressed as a sum of AdS$_{3}$ single-trace Witten diagrams, where the internal propagators correspond to spinning primaries with specific spins. These spins are determined by the conformal dimensions of the external operators and the total dimension of the OPE block. We also explore the connection between this result and the spinning AdS$_{3}$ Witten equation.

Lobster-eye optics, which utilize the principle of total external reflection, are highly effective for detecting X-rays across extensive fields of view. This study introduces a novel concept for enhancing the detection capabilities of lobster-eye optics by integrating multiple distinct optical axes into a single module. This approach allows for the simultaneous observation of multiple regions within the sky. The paper outlines the design of a prototype module featuring three separate optical axes and presents simulation results demonstrating the module's performance. These simulations indicate that the multiplexed design achieves a detection efficiency comparable to that of a single-axis module, while significantly expanding the observable sky area. The authors conclude that this technology holds substantial promise for applications requiring wide-field X-ray monitoring.

Dark matter halos serve as the primary gravitational structures in the universe, hosting galaxies and their associated gas reservoirs. Consequently, the relationship between halo mass and observable properties—known as the mass function—is a critical area of study. While numerous methods exist to reconstruct this function from galaxy surveys, they typically rely on the assumption that the observed distribution of dark matter reflects the underlying density field. This paper challenges that assumption by demonstrating that the cosmic velocity field significantly influences the observed dark matter distribution. We show that neglecting this velocity component leads to systematic errors in reconstructing the mass function. To address this, we introduce a deep learning framework designed to recover the dark matter mass function from galaxy survey data while explicitly accounting for the cosmic velocity field. Our results indicate that incorporating velocity information substantially improves reconstruction accuracy, particularly at high masses where the velocity field's impact is most pronounced.

This study demonstrates the capability of atomic interferometry to detect minute local magnetic field variations by leveraging the Meissner effect in superconductors. We achieved this by measuring the phase shift in an atom interferometer caused by a magnetic field generated when a superconducting lead (Pb) sphere was cooled below its critical temperature. The resulting phase shift was measured at 0.01 rad, corresponding to a local magnetic field change of 0.01 G. This sensitivity surpasses the detection limit of a standard SQUID magnetometer by a factor of 100. The findings suggest that combining atomic interferometry with superconductors offers a highly sensitive method for detecting local magnetic field changes.

We present a relativistic first-principles investigation into the electronic characteristics of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states, which emerge from magnetic adatoms and their associated dimers situated on superconducting surfaces. Our analysis focuses on an Mn adatom and Mn dimers on Nb(110), utilizing a relativistic formalism that incorporates spin-orbit coupling within the Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian. The resulting electronic structures are examined through the density of states (DOS) and differential conductance ($dI/dV$) spectra. We find that the calculated $dI/dV$ results align well with experimental observations, specifically reproducing the characteristic zero-bias conductance peaks and the distinctive splitting of the Shiba resonance. Furthermore, our study reveals that the Shiba resonance splitting is primarily driven by the local magnetic environment of the Mn adatom and its dimer configurations.

Skin cancer detection is a critical task in medical image analysis, yet it faces significant challenges due to the scarcity of labeled data and the presence of outliers in existing datasets. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to address these issues by integrating an entropy-based outlier detection mechanism. The proposed method employs a two-stage process: first, a pre-trained ResNet50 model is fine-tuned on the ISIC 2018 dataset to learn robust feature representations; second, these features are processed through a one-class SVM classifier to identify and remove anomalous samples. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively eliminates outliers, leading to enhanced detection performance. Specifically, the method achieves an accuracy of 90.4% on the ISIC 2018 dataset and 91.5% on the ISIC 2019 dataset.

At high-energy muon colliders, the process of producing vector bosons via muon collisions is well-suited for an effective theory approach. This paper introduces the Effective W Approximation (EWA) specifically designed for muon colliders, which is derived from the full electroweak theory. The study examines the accuracy of this approximation across various scattering processes, including both $2\to2$ and $2\to3$ events. Results indicate that the EWA performs reliably at high energies for $2\to2$ processes, with deviations from the exact electroweak calculation remaining below 10% for the specific case of $W^+W^-\to t\bar{b}$. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the EWA remains effective for $2\to3$ processes, provided that the additional radiation is emitted at large angles relative to the incoming muons.

This paper presents a novel demonstration of the fact that the Rosser sentence is not equivalent to the standard Godel sentence, a result that relies on the assumption of the consistency of Peano Arithmetic. The demonstration is constructed using only elementary logical principles, requiring no advanced arithmetization techniques. The authors argue that this approach offers a more direct and conceptually transparent alternative to the original proof by Carnap and Rosser.

Invariant manifolds are fundamental to the analysis of dynamical systems, serving as essential tools for understanding the global behavior of solutions. This paper demonstrates that invariant manifolds do not exist for fractional order dynamical systems. The proof is established by showing that the fractional order derivative of a function defined on an invariant manifold cannot be expressed as a function of the function itself and its fractional order derivatives.

This study examines the inverse problem associated with a structural acoustic interaction, where the objective is to determine the unknown boundary impedance of a vibrating plate. The analysis establishes the existence and uniqueness of the solution for this problem, alongside the derivation of a stability estimate. Furthermore, the paper introduces a regularization strategy designed to address the ill-posed nature of the problem.

We examine the minimal scoto-seesaw framework, focusing on the phenomenology of neutrino masses, dark matter, and Higgs vacuum stability. In this model, the neutrino mass matrix is generated through the interaction of a scalar singlet with the Standard Model Higgs doublet, while the neutrino mass scale is determined by the mass of the heavy right-handed neutrinos. We demonstrate that the dark matter candidate, a stable neutral component of the scalar singlet, can simultaneously satisfy dark matter relic density constraints and direct detection limits from XENON1T. Furthermore, we show that the model can account for the observed neutrino mass scale and mixing parameters while ensuring vacuum stability up to the Planck scale.
